QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: This matches behavior described when the robot approaches a singularity: the arm can stop moving or have very sudden and fast movements if it approaches a singularity. Singularity also makes the arm feel heavy to position. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

How to prevent it:
- Avoid programming motions that result in any poses that can cause a singularity. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- During installation/programming, consider workspace/operating space and do not move the tool close to the cylindrical volume directly above or below the base (robot extends 850 mm from base). Moving the tool close to the cylindrical volume can cause joints to move too fast. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Use proper risk assessment and safe motion planning (keep trajectories away from singular poses). Read and follow the installation and programming guidance in the User Manual. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

If you need help identifying a specific singularity in your program, say so and provide the motion/pose details.

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE (3-Position Enabling) buttons on the Teach Pendant provide manual hold-to-run and mode-control functions in Manual mode: [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

- Position 1 (Release): no pressure — robot movement is stopped in Manual mode (power retained, brakes released).  
- Position 2 (Light‑press / middle): allows programs to play and enables Freedrive or automated moves while held (used to run or continue a program).  
- Position 3 (Tight‑press / full): robot movement is stopped in Manual mode (3PE Stop).  

Additional behaviours:
- The 3PE buttons are only active in Manual mode; they have no effect in Automatic mode.  
- Rapid light‑press, release, light‑press and hold sequence enables Freedrive for manually pulling the arm. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After any modification, verify required safety level and correct functioning of all safety functions, and conduct checks in accordance with national/regional work safety regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Unplug main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources before working; prevent others from powering the system during repair. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Check the earth connection before re-powering the system and observe ESD regulations when parts are disassembled. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Test stopping performance periodically (stopping time/distance) and ensure any safety-rated stops and safety functions operate correctly. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- For commissioning after modifications, verify all safety inputs/outputs, emergency stop buttons and enabling devices, safeguard inputs, operational mode changes, and any system outputs (Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, etc.) function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple

Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.

motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.

verify that there is a stop of the whole system.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources, and take precautions to prevent others from powering the system during maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Check the earth (ground) connection before re-powering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Observe ESD regulations when parts of the robot arm or Control Box are disassembled. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box during maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Avoid disassembling the Control Box power supply too quickly after switching off because high voltages (up to 600 V) can be present for several hours. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Follow all safety instructions in the manual and perform inspections/repairs according to the Service Manual; repair work should be done by Universal Robots or trained, authorized personnel following the Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Additional general safety reminders:
- Verify the robot arm and tool/end effector are properly and securely bolted in place and avoid using the robot if damaged. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Inform users of emergency stop locations and warn people to keep outside the robot reach during work. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the tool attachments I can put on the universal robot relating to moving objects with the arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: The robot can have an end effector (also referred to as the tool or the workpiece) mounted to the tool output flange to allow the robot to manipulate a workpiece — examples include grippers and sensors used on a specific robot tool. (Terminology and mounting details) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]

Supporting notes:
- The tool is mounted to the tool flange (ISO 9409-1) at Wrist 3; use appropriate bolts (do not exceed 10 mm length) and a radially slotted hole for the positioning pin is recommended [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- The tool connector provides power and control signals for grippers and sensors (8-pin tool connector / tool cable adapter; pins include digital I/O, analog I/O, power, RS485) and must be tightened to max 0.4 Nm. Configure tool I/O power (0V/12V/24V) in Installation settings [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Ensure the tool is securely bolted and constructed so parts cannot drop unexpectedly; follow end-effector-specific documentation for mounting and connection [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
STUDENT ANSWER: The robot can suffer permanent damage or unexpected behaviors from very high electromagnetic signal levels or excessive exposure (EMC problems are often seen in welding processes and typically show up as error messages in the log). To avoid this:

- Keep I/O cable lengths from the Control Box to other machinery ≤ 30 m unless additional tests are performed.  
- Read and follow the Electrical Interface chapter and use correct gland sizes and cable installations to avoid introducing EMC issues.

QUESTION: What are the steps for moving the robot arm safely to check its position stability?
STUDENT ANSWER: The sources do not present a single step-by-step checklist titled exactly "moving the robot arm safely to check its position stability." However, relevant instructions and required precautions are provided in the retrieved documents. Key steps and safety points you should follow are:

- Power up and select appropriate mode:
  - Enable power (press ON) and use Manual/Backdrive or Freedrive depending on need (see Backdrive/Enable Backdrive procedure) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

- Use Freedrive or Move tab to move the arm:
  - Use the Move tab arrows or hold the on-screen Freedrive button to move the robot arm; Translate arrows move the TCP, Rotate arrows change tool orientation about the TCP [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part02_part02.pdf].
  - Alternatively, hold the physical Freedrive to pull the arm into position (Freedrive must be enabled appropriately) [010__L1__10...part01.pdf; 013__L1__13...pdf].

- Verify installation and payload settings before Freedrive:
  - Ensure correct robot mounting angle, payload mass and payload center of gravity offset, and save/load the installation files with the program; incorrect settings can cause unwanted movement or risk of arm falling during Freedrive [010__L1__10...part02_part02.pdf].

- Keep personnel outside the robot reach during Freedrive:
  - All personnel shall remain outside the reach (workspace) of the robot arm when Freedrive is in use; Freedrive shall only be used if allowed by the risk assessment [010__L1__10...part02_part02.pdf].

- If using Backdrive (manual movement with brakes engaged):
  - Follow the Backdrive enabling sequence (3PE Teach Pendant, 3PE device/switch, or Freedrive); the arm will feel heavy and you must apply significant force to move joints [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].
  - Test Backdrive on all joints and verify safety settings comply with the installation risk assessment; check that additional safety inputs/outputs are still functioning [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

- During movement and checks:
  - Compare the on‑screen animation with the real robot to ensure the movement can be performed without collision (Move Robot into Position guidance) [010__L1__10...part01.pdf].
  - Do not move joints more than 160° when moving without drive power; do not move any joint more than necessary (Movement Without Drive Power) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].
  - Use caution in Recovery Mode because some limits are disabled; move back within limits carefully [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

- Emergency stop and reset procedure if needed:
  - If required, press the Teach Pendant E‑stop to stop motion; to reset twist the button clockwise after visually assessing the cause and resolving it before restoring power [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

QUESTION: How can I set up my active program so that I only need to modify 1 or 2 variables each run?
STUDENT ANSWER: You can use program and installation variables so your program logic reads a small set of inputs each run (e.g., 1–2 variables) and the program uses those to control behavior.

How to do this (from PolyScope):
- Create variables in the Program header (Program variables) or in Installation → Variables (installation variables) and give them meaningful descriptions. Program variables belong to a program; installation variables can be shared among programs. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]
- Mark the variables you will change frequently as Favorite variables in Variable Setup (Header → Program or Header → Installation → Variables) so they are shown easily in the Run tab. In Run, check "Show only favorite variables" to display only those variables. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]
- In your program use those variables (in If, Wait, loop conditions, or to set I/O/actions) so changing those 1–2 variables is sufficient to alter program behavior. All program and installation variables are displayed in the Run tab when you play the program. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

Optional convenience:
- Name variables clearly (user-defined names) so they are easy to edit from the I/O/Variables screens. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]
- Use the Run tab to monitor and edit the displayed favorite variables at runtime. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

Sources: [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf], [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot is close to a collision and if I restart it, it may cause another collision from the vibrations. What can I do?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use Backdrive to force specific joints to the desired position without releasing all brakes, so you can move the arm away from the close-collision position without a full restart vibration. Backdrive can be enabled via the 3PE Teach Pendant, an external 3PE device/switch, or Freedrive on robot; while Backdrive is active the joints will feel heavy to move and you must apply significant pressure to release the brakes [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

Short supporting points:
- Use the 3PE Teach Pendant sequence (light-press then light-press-and-hold 3PE TP button after ON) to enter Backdrive, or press-and-hold a configured 3PE device/switch, or press-and-hold Freedrive on robot [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].
- In Backdrive mode the robot is “heavy” to move; test Backdrive on all joints and verify safety settings before moving the arm [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].
- If you need to move the arm manually without power, forced back-driving can be used but requires high force and often two or more people; always support the arm before removing power and do not move joints more than necessary or more than 160° [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

QUESTION: I dropped some liquid on my robot arm. Will that break it or cause a safety issue?
STUDENT ANSWER: Short answer: Probably not — the robot arm is rated IP54, so light splashes/droplets are tolerated, but exposure to strong or prolonged liquid may cause damage or safety issues. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]

Supporting points:
- The Teach Pendant and robot arm touch surfaces are designed for industrial environments and the touch screen resists water droplets and machine coolant droplets (use tip of finger or stylus for input) — indicating some protection against small liquid exposure. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf]
- The robot arm has an IP54 classification (protection against limited dust ingress and splashing water); however, the manual warns that prolonged contact with heat or other environmental extremes can cause issues and that very strong magnetic fields and other exposures can damage the robot. If the liquid caused contamination, corrosion, or electrical faults, that could create hazards. [002__L1__2._Your_Robot__pp12-27.pdf] 
- Recommended actions: power down and visually inspect the robot and connectors; remove any pooled liquid, allow the robot to dry fully before powering on, and perform a functional and safety check (including emergency stop and safety inputs). If you cannot verify it is safe, contact support. The manual emphasizes performing risk assessments and avoiding use if the robot is damaged. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Define safety planes and tool position limits, and enable elbow and/or tool flange restrictions in Safety settings.

- Create a plane feature (or copy Base/Undefined) in Installation > Features, then in Installation > Safety > Planes add a safety plane and enable "Restrict Elbow" and/or "Tool Flange Restriction" as needed to prevent the elbow or tool flange crossing the plane [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Set up Tool Position (Installation > Safety > Tool Position): define the tool TCPs and give each tool an appropriate Radius and Position; safety planes use the tool sphere and the tool TCP when enforcing and triggering limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Configure plane Modes (Normal, Reduced, Trigger Reduced) so the plane acts as a strict positional limit or to switch to Reduced mode when crossed; use up to eight planes and set which side is allowed by the plane arrow [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

Notes/warnings:
- Safety planes only limit the defined tool spheres and elbow, not every robot part; they do not guarantee other arm parts obey the restriction [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].
- Define features and tool TCPs before unlocking Safety (the robot powers off when Safety is unlocked) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: If the robot arm is moving slowly or stopping even though it is not near anything, likely causes from the manual are:

- The active safety limits (e.g., Stopping Time/Distance, Speed Limit, Joint Speed Limit, or Reduced mode) are restricting motion — the safety system dynamically reduces speed so the robot can stop within the configured limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

- The robot may be in Reduced or Recovery mode:
  - Reduced mode applies more restrictive limits when triggered by a trigger plane or safety input and can reduce speed for safety reasons [010__L1__10...pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10...pp107-120.pdf].
  - Recovery mode activates if a safety limit was already violated at power-up; in Recovery the robot can be moved but many limits are disabled and movement is constrained by fixed Recovery limits (e.g., Speed Limit 250 mm/s, Joint Speed Limit 30°/s). Recovery also prevents running programs [010__L1__10...pp107-120.pdf; 013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

- A safety stop input (Emergency Stop, Safeguard Stop, 3PE Stop) may be asserted or a safety fault detected; different stop categories cause stops or pauses and safety outputs go low when triggered [010__L1__10...pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10...pp105-106.pdf].

What to check (based on the manual):
- Verify which Safety Mode is active (Normal, Reduced, or Recovery) and whether a Trigger Reduced Plane or a safety input is causing Reduced mode [010__L1__10...pp106-112.pdf].
- Check the Safety Checksum / Safety Configuration to confirm no unintended changes were applied and that settings match the risk assessment [010__L1__10...pp107-112.pdf].
- Inspect safety inputs/outputs and confirm no Emergency Stop, Safeguard Stop, or other safety inputs are active or faulted (safety outputs reset to low on faults) [010__L1__10...pp104-106.pdf; 008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf].
- If the robot started in Recovery mode, move the arm back within limits using Freedrive or Move tab, then recover (programs cannot run during Recovery) [010__L1__10...pp107-120.pdf; 013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf].

If these checks do not identify the cause, the manual does not provide further troubleshooting steps in the retrieved sections.

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Most likely causes from the manual:

- Resonance between the robot and its stand (insufficient dynamic stiffness). The stand should have a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz; if eigenfrequency matches robot movement frequency the system can resonate and appear to vibrate. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

- Loose or insufficiently secured mounting (deflection or vibration). Ensure the robot is secured to a sturdy, vibration-free surface and tightened with the specified M8 bolts to 20 Nm. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

- Control Box or environment issues: inadequate Control Box clearance or overheating airflow can cause malfunctioning behaviour—ensure minimum 50 mm clearance (200 mm recommended) and no contact with liquids. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

- During startup/release of brakes the robot may vibrate slightly (normal); also backdrive/freedrive behaviour or being close to collision can produce vibrations. Verify mounting, payload and that brakes/release sequence are correct. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf] [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

If these checks do not explain the vibration, the manuals do not provide additional troubleshooting steps in the retrieved pages.

QUESTION: Are there risks associated with using 12V vs 24V?
STUDENT ANSWER: Yes — there are electrical risks when using 12V vs 24V. The manual warns that programmer and/or wiring errors can cause the voltage to change from 12V to 24V, which can lead to fire damage to equipment; verify the use of 12V and proceed with caution. Also note tool power supply guidance: Tool I/O can be set to 0V, 12V or 24V and supply current/peak limits apply; tool power is turned to 0V after an Emergency Stop. Use the Installation settings and follow the electrical specifications to avoid damage. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the manual)
- The robot approached or entered a singularity, which can make motion resistive and then produce very sudden and fast movements as it is approached or left. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- A safety limit violation or safety-system stop (Recovery mode) occurred and then the robot was moved out of limits (or restarted), during which limits such as joint position, tool position and tool orientation are disabled — allowing hazardous motion while returning to limits. Recovery mode also allows limited joint speeds but can produce unexpected motion if not handled carefully. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- A sudden change in configured safety limits (e.g., switching between Normal and Reduced mode, or applying new Safety Configuration) can change allowable speeds/momentum and cause abrupt motion if not confirmed/applied correctly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

How to prevent recurrence
- Avoid programming motions that produce singularities; plan trajectories to keep clear of singular poses. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Perform a complete application risk assessment and set appropriate safety configuration settings (speed, force, momentum, joint limits, safety planes, stopping time/distance) per the integrator’s assessment; protect safety settings with a password so they cannot be changed by unauthorized users. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Use and verify the safety limits (Joint limits, Safety Planes, Tool Orientation, Speed/Force/Momentum/Power limits) to restrict motions and reduce energy transfer in collisions; apply and confirm changes (Apply and Restart) so the Safety Checksum reflects the active configuration. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- When recovering from a stop or using Recovery mode, move the arm cautiously (use Freedrive or Move tab) and remember that some limits are disabled in Recovery; follow the Recovery-mode speed/force limits and support the arm if removing power. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Ensure mounting, payload and installation settings are correct (incorrect mounting/payload can cause unexpected motion or tipping) and verify joint acceleration/stand stiffness to reduce dynamic issues. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf] [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

If you need, tell me:
- What the robot state/message was at the time (e.g., Recovery, Safeguard Stop, Emergency Stop, fault).
- Whether you had recently changed safety settings, installation/mounting, or the robot program.

QUESTION: Can you describe the robot stop categories?
STUDENT ANSWER: Stop categories are defined per IEC 60204-1 and the UR5e implements three types:

- Stop Category 0: Stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Stop Category 1: Stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Stop Category 2: Stop the robot while maintaining drive power; drive power is maintained after the robot is stopped. Universal Robots’ Category 2 stops are further described as SS1 or SS2 type stops according to IEC 61800-5-2. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: The sources do not provide a single consolidated “after modifying the robot arm” checklist, but they do specify required checks and procedures you must follow after maintenance, repair or modifications:

- Perform inspections and maintenance in compliance with all safety instructions and local requirements, and follow the latest Service Manual for maintenance, inspection, calibration and repair work; repair work should only be done by Universal Robots or trained individuals following the Service Manual [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- After maintenance and repair work, checks must be done to ensure the required safety level; checks must adhere to applicable national/regional work safety regulations and the correct functioning of all safety functions must be tested [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources before working; ensure earth connection before re‑powering; observe ESD regulations; prevent water/dust ingress; do not disassemble the Control Box power supply too soon after switch‑off due to residual high voltages (up to 600 V) [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Test stopping performance periodically (and after changes) to determine if stopping performance is degraded; if stop time/distance functions are used as the risk reduction strategy the robot does continuous monitoring so no extra testing is required [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Follow the Robot Arm Inspection Plan: perform the listed inspections at the indicated intervals (monthly, biannually, annually) and rectify/replace any parts found unacceptable (examples: check flat rings, robot cable and connections, mounting bolts, tool mounting bolts, round sling) [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Specific inspection steps (example procedure): move robot to ZERO if possible; turn off and disconnect power cable from Control Box; inspect cable between Control Box and Robot Arm; check base mounting bolts and tool flange bolts; inspect flat rings for wear/damage and replace if worn/damaged [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- Do not use compressed air to clean the robot arm (can damage components) [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

- If you changed safety‑related settings or hardware, conduct commissioning checks before first use or after modifications: verify all safety inputs/outputs are correctly connected; test all connected safety inputs/outputs (including devices common to multiple machines); test emergency stop buttons/inputs to verify robot stops and brakes engage; test safeguard inputs and any safeguard reset; verify operational mode indications and 3‑position enabling device behavior as applicable; determine commissioning requirements for your application [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf].

- If safety configuration was changed, ensure changes comply with the integrator’s risk assessment, apply and restart to visually inspect Safety Configuration (SI units popup), then Confirm Safety Configuration; verify Safety Checksum if needed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

- After repairs, save and review logs/error reports as needed (Log tab shows system info; you can save error reports and support files for diagnostics) [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf].

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources, and take measures to prevent others from re-powering the system during maintenance. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- The tool connector provides power and control signals for grippers and sensors (pins include digital inputs/outputs, analog inputs, RS485, power and ground); the tool connector must be tightened to 0.4 Nm [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Configure tool I/O power (0V / 12V / 24V), digital I/O modes (sinking/sourcing/push‑pull), and tool power according to the Installation → Tool I/O settings before use [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety state in which the robot uses a distinct (more restrictive) set of safety limits (Normal and Reduced are available) — e.g., joint position, joint speed, TCP pose, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time and stopping distance are set to the Reduced values. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf] 

Reduced Mode is activated when:
- the robot Tool Center Point (TCP) (or configured tool point) is positioned beyond a Trigger Reduced-mode plane, or

4. Move the arm using the recommended interfaces (Move tab / Move Robot into Position / Freedrive):

6. Use low speeds and conservative settings during checks.
   - Do not increase speed/acceleration above defaults for testing; for manual hand-guiding, set tool/elbow speed ≤ 250 mm/s unless risk assessment allows otherwise. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf; 010__L1__10...__pp99-106.pdf]

7. If safety limits or faults occur, follow Recovery / Backdrive guidance:

Recovery safety limits: joint speed 30°/s, tool speed 250 mm/s, force 100 N, momentum 10 kg·m/s, power 80 W. 8. After moving, verify stability and secure setup:
   - Ensure robot is on a sturdy mount, stand appropriately dimensioned, and Control Box clearance is respected; re-check mounting bolts and stand stiffness if positional instability is observed. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the network configuration requirements to use the network features of the robot?
STUDENT ANSWER: Network configuration requirements to use the robot’s network features (based on the provided sources):

- The robot supports Fieldbus options: MODBUS, Ethernet/IP, PROFINET, and PROFIsafe. You configure these through PolyScope Fieldbus settings. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]
- For MODBUS, you create MODBUS units and signals with specific IP addresses; you can set signal types (digital input/output, register input/output) and manage connections, updates, and advanced options (including update frequency and slave address). Ensure the remote MODBUS device addresses and values are valid. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]
- PROFIsafe requires connection to a safety-compliant PLC on a trusted network; enabling PROFIsafe involves unlocking in Safety settings, entering source/destination addresses, and optionally enabling operational mode control via PROFIsafe. A safety password is required to unlock, and only one source can control the robot’s operational mode when PROFIsafe is enabled. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

Notes:
- Ensure the robot is connected to a trusted, properly secured network for these features. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]
- The EtherNet/IP and PROFINET options include handling losses of connection by choosing None, Pause, or Stop actions in PolyScope. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Based on the Safety Functions in 10.2.1 and Safety I/O materials:

- The robot may slow down or stop due to safety limits being active. Safety functions like Stopping Time Limit and Stopping Distance Limit can dynamically reduce motion to ensure the robot can stop within the configured limits. If a limit is exceeded, a Stop Category 0 can occur. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- If Recovery mode is active ( Recovery limits ), or if any safety limit violation is detected, the safety system may halt or constrain motion. Recovery mode uses lower limits and requires restart. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__10.2.3._Safety Parameter Set__pp105-106.pdf]

- Ensure you have no active Safety Planes or excessive joint/speed/force limits configured that would unnecessarily constrain motion; verify Normal configuration vs Reduced configuration and any triggering inputs. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__10.2.1._Configurable Safety Functions__pp100-101.pdf]

- If an Emergency Stop or Safeguard Stop has been triggered, the robot will stop or pause; check Safety inputs/outputs and any connected safety devices. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf]

- Recovery requires manual movement back within limits or Freedrive; until recovered, motion may be restricted. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp105-107.pdf]

If you’ve already run risk assessment, these safety features can still trigger due to dynamic stopping logic; review the Safety Parameters, Stopping Time/Distance limits, and any active Safety configuration in PolyScope. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?

- Avoid actions that could push the robot toward a singularity or cause unsafe moves; plan trajectories within defined safety limits and use safety planes/joint limits to constrain motion. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE buttons provide manual control and safety functions when using Manual mode:

- Button 1 (Release): no pressure; robot movement is stopped in Manual mode, brakes remain released.
- Button 2 (Light-press): light pressure; allows program to play (run) in Manual mode.

Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What are the network configuration requirements to use the network features of the robot?
STUDENT ANSWER: Network configuration requirements for UR5e:

- Connect the robot to a trusted network that accesses required services (e.g., safety PLC for PROFIsafe) and enable fieldbus options as needed. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

- Supported fieldbus protocols you can configure: MODBUS, Ethernet/IP, PROFINET, and PROFIsafe. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

- For PROFIsafe, you must configure through PolyScope Safety settings and enable PROFIsafe after unlocking Safety parameters; you also set source and destination addresses for safety communication. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

- Ensure you have proper licensing for PROFIsafe (UR5e with enabling license obtained via UR sales) and load it via myUR as applicable. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

- When configuring MODBUS, you manage units, IPs, signals (digital I/O, registers), and can observe signal status and statistics; network reachability and TCP/IP are involved. [012__L1__12._Communication_Networks__pp171-180.pdf]

STUDENT ANSWER: To keep the elbow and tool inside a defined area, use Safety Planes and Tool/Elbow Restrictions in Software Safety. Specifically:

- Enable Tool Flange Restriction to prevent the tool flange from crossing a safety plane, with an unrestricted area inside the plane. - Ensure Tool Position and Plane features are configured before unlocking Safety, and use the Safety Configuration (Normal/Reduced) to enforce limits during operation. QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible reason: Safety configuration may be in Normal vs Reduced mode or Recovery mode, which slows or stops movement after a start if safety limits are engaged.

- The safety system can operate in Normal or Reduced mode, and can automatically transition to Reduced mode based on tool position or input triggers. When Reduced mode is active, speed and other limits are tighter, causing slower motion or stops [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- Recovery Mode activates when a safety limit is violated; in Recovery Mode the robot can move but with restricted limits, and certain safety functions are disabled (joint position/limits disabled in Recovery). This can cause slowdowns or halted motion until you move back within limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- Ensure you are not in a safety configuration that automatically reduces speed or triggers a safety stop. You can check and adjust Normal/Reduced modes and verify Safety Checksum in PolyScope to confirm current safety configuration, and apply/restart as needed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

If after risk assessment you expect normal operation, verify:
- Safety parameters in Normal mode are configured per the risk assessment, and that you are not in Reduced or Recovery mode due to a trigger or fault [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- There are no active safety inputs forcing Reduced mode; check Safety I/O configuration and Ensure safety inputs/outputs are correct per Safety I/O guidance [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-70.pdf]. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Based on the provided sources, a strong, sudden movement after a stop could be related to recovery/recovery mode or safety-related events.

- Possible causes:
  - Safety system invoked Stop Category 0 due to a safety limit violation, fault, or recovery condition (Safety Functions and Recovery Mode described in 10.2, 10.2.2, and 10.2.3 in UR5e First Time Use; see Safety Functions and Recovery Mode details). This can cause the robot to move abruptly when limits are violated or when recovering.
  - Recovery Mode activated when a safety limit is exceeded; during Recovery, limits are fixed and movement can feel heavy until back within limits (Recovery Mode section under 10.2.3). 
  - A Safeguard Stop or Emergency Stop could have been triggered, leading to a stop, then a rapid re-acceleration when allowed (Safety Functions table shows Stop categories and responses in 10.2.2 and 10.2.3).

- How to prevent:
  - Ensure risk assessment is performed and safety configuration settings are appropriate (see 4 Risk Assessment and 10.2 Safety-related Functions and Interfaces; Safety Configuration and Password protection in 10.3 and 10.2.1). 
  - Verify safety limits and mode configuration before operation, including Normal vs Reduced modes and the use of Safety Planes and Joint/Tool limits as defined in Safety Configuration (10.2.3, 10.2.1, 10.3.1).
  - Confirm all emergency stop sources and I/O are correctly configured, and that the system restarts safely after a stop (Emergency Events 13.1, 10.2.2).
  - Maintain proper mounting, installation, and payload settings so Freedrive and Normal operation don’t provoke unexpected movements (Assembly sections on mounting and payload considerations, e.g., 6.4 Securing the Robot Arm and 10.5 Move/Freedrive cautions).

Key references:
- 10. First Time Use: Safety-related Functions and Interfaces; Safety Parameter Sets; Recovery Mode; Safety limits (UR5e First Time Use, 10.2–10.2.3, 10.3). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- 13. Emergency Events: Emergency Stop and Backdrive details (Emergency Stop, Recovery/Backdrive behavior) [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- 4. Risk Assessment: importance of risk assessment and safety configuration settings [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- 10. First Time Use: Software Safety Configuration and enabling safety passwords (to prevent unintended changes) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- 013 Emergency Events also covers manual movement restrictions during E-stop and recovery [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Yes, there is a list of tests to conduct after making a modification to the robot arm. 
Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple
machines or robots, are functioning as intended.
Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Before performing maintenance on a UR robot arm, follow these safety precautions from the Safety and Maintenance sections:

- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box; take precautions to prevent others from powering on during maintenance. Check the earth connection before re-powering. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Observe ESD regulations when disassembling parts of the robot arm or Control Box; prevent water and dust ingress. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Disassembly of the Power supply inside the Control Box can expose high voltages (up to 600 V) for hours after shutdown; avoid disassembling it. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Use appropriate PPE and safe cleaning/handling procedures for maintenance tasks (see cleaning/grease sections for safety guidance). [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- After maintenance, perform checks to ensure required safety level and test the correct functioning of all safety functions. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: The safety settings in the configuration wont let me change certain settings? Why not?
STUDENT ANSWER: If certain safety settings cannot be changed, it is because the software safety settings are password‑protected and/or the robot is in a safety mode that restricts editing or movement.

Key reasons from the sources:
- Safety Settings are locked until a Safety password is set and used; you must Unlock with the Safety password to make settings accessible [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].  
- When the Safety Tab is unlocked, the robot is powered off and changes only take effect after you tap Apply and Restart; you cannot power the robot on until Apply and Restart is selected [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].  
- Some limits/settings are constrained by the active Safety Mode (Normal, Reduced, Recovery). Recovery mode (entered when a safety limit is violated or at startup if a limit is already violated) disables joint/tool/orientation limits and restricts movement, and certain safety limits are fixed in Recovery—you cannot customize them until recovery is cleared [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].  
- Safety planes, tool definitions and other safety items are feature‑based; you must create required Features/Tools before editing corresponding safety plane or tool direction/position settings (otherwise configuration options are restricted or show warnings) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- Some settings are intentionally limited by default for safety (e.g., factory presets, limits on speeds/forces) and changes must comply with the integrator’s risk assessment; unauthorized or unsupported changes are prevented to avoid hazardous situations [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

If you still cannot change a specific setting, check that:
- You have set and entered the Safety password and unlocked the Safety screen [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].  
- You have created/defined required Features, Tools or TCPs used by that safety setting (e.g., safety plane needs a plane feature; tool direction needs a feature; tool position needs a defined tool) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].  
- The robot is not in Recovery mode due to a limit violation (clear recovery by moving the robot back within limits using Freedrive or Move after unlocking) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

If none of the above explain your issue, state which specific setting is locked and I will reference the relevant section.

QUESTION: My robot is close to a collision and if I restart it, it may cause another collision from the vibrations. What can I do?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use Backdrive to move the robot arm to a safe position without releasing all brakes, so you avoid vibrations from a full restart. Backdrive can be enabled via the 3PE Teach Pendant, a configured 3PE device/switch, or Freedrive on the robot, and lets you apply significant pressure to release individual joint brakes and move the arm (see "Backdrive" and "Backdrive on robot" procedures). [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Backdrive is intended for situations where the arm is close to collision and vibrations from a full restart are undesirable; the joints will feel heavy to move while Backdrive is in use. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Mandatory: test Backdrive on all joints and verify safety settings and additional safety inputs/outputs before use. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- If power is unavailable, you can also perform forced back-driving by physically pushing/pulling the arm, but this requires high force and often two or more people and risks — support the arm before removing power. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: If the robot starts slowly or stops even though it is not near anything, the safety system is likely restricting motion because one of its safety limits or modes is active.

Possible causes (from sources):
- The safety system is in Reduced or Recovery mode, which applies more restrictive limits (Reduced) or fixed recovery limits and disables some limits (Recovery). Recovery activates if a safety limit is violated at power-up or during use, and it restricts motion (e.g., joint speed 30°/s, tool speed 250 mm/s, force 100 N, momentum 10 kg·m/s, power 80 W) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- A configured Trigger Reduced Plane or a safety input may have switched the system to Reduced mode; Reduced mode enforces more restrictive speed/momentum limits and the robot transitions within 500 ms after the trigger [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- If a safety limit is violated or a fault detected, the controller issues a Stop Category 0 and safety outputs reset; the safety system may be preventing program motion until Recovery is completed or limits are restored [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].
- Stopping Time/Distance limits or other configured speed limits can dynamically reduce robot speed so it can always stop within the set limits; tighter stopping time/distance settings reduce allowable speed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

- Verify which Safety Mode is active (Normal, Reduced, or Recovery) in the Safety Configuration and the Safety Checksum to see if safety settings changed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- Inspect configured Trigger Reduced Planes and any safety inputs (e.g., Reduced input, 3-position enabling, Freedrive input) that can cause Reduced mode [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf].

Recovery activates if a safety limit is violated at power-up or during use, and it restricts motion (e.g., joint speed 30°/s, tool speed 250 mm/s, force 100 N, momentum 10 kg·m/s, power 80 W) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- A configured Trigger Reduced Plane or a safety input may have switched the system to Reduced mode; Reduced mode enforces more restrictive speed/momentum limits and the robot transitions within 500 ms after the trigger [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- If a safety limit is violated or a fault detected, the controller issues a Stop Category 0 and safety outputs reset; the safety system may be preventing program motion until Recovery is completed or limits are restored [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].
- Stopping Time/Distance limits or other configured speed limits can dynamically reduce robot speed so it can always stop within the set limits; tighter stopping time/distance settings reduce allowable speed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

What to check (recommended from sources):
- Verify which Safety Mode is active (Normal, Reduced, or Recovery) in the Safety Configuration and the Safety Checksum to see if safety settings changed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- Inspect configured Trigger Reduced Planes and any safety inputs (e.g., Reduced input, 3-position enabling, Freedrive input) that can cause Reduced mode [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf].
- Check if a safety limit was violated at start-up (Recovery mode). If in Recovery, move the arm back within limits using Freedrive or Move tab, taking caution because some limits are disabled in Recovery [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- Review Stopping Time/Distance, Speed Limit, Tool/Elbow speed and joint speed limit settings in the Safety Configuration; more restrictive values reduce maximum motion speed [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: The robot (or entire system) can appear to vibrate if the stand lacks sufficient dynamic stiffness so its natural frequency matches the robot motion frequency, causing resonance. Ensure the stand has a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz and is sufficiently stiff (static and dynamic stiffness) to avoid deflection or resonance. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Also check for singularities: as the arm approaches a singularity it can feel heavy or behave with sudden/fast motions. Avoid programming motions that result in singularity poses. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: How can I reduce the force applied to the operator in case of a collision?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use the robot’s Power and Force Limiting and related safety limits in the Safety Configuration to reduce force in a collision. Specifically:

- Configure Force and Power Limiting (Tool Force / Elbow Force) to limit maximum force exerted by the tool and elbow [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Use Momentum Limits and Speed Limitation (Tool Speed / Elbow Speed) to reduce transient energy and impact forces by limiting robot momentum and speed [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].  
- Apply joint, elbow and tool/end effector position and orientation limits to avoid motions or exposures that increase injury risk (e.g., avoid moving toward head/neck or pointing sharp edges toward operator) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  

Make these changes via the Software Safety Configuration per the integrator’s application risk assessment and protect the safety settings with a Safety password [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the sources)
- Approaching a singularity: as the robot approaches a singularity pose it can stop moving or have very sudden and fast movements (singularity resistance increases and motion can become abrupt). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Stopping and restarting behavior / joint torques during stops: during stopping motion joints may exceed maximum nominal operating torque and generate high loads; improper handling of stops could lead to sudden motion when power/brakes change state. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Incorrect Move into Position or program start pose: Move Robot into Position can move the arm to an incorrect pose if TCP/feature/waypoint pose of the first movement was altered during execution or the first waypoint is inside an If/Switch node — unexpected repositioning could produce abrupt motion. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

How to prevent it (actions from the sources)
- Avoid singularities in programming and motion planning: do not program motions that result in poses that can cause a singularity. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Verify program start positions and use Move Robot into Position safely:
  - Ensure the robot is in the program’s first start position before playing programs.
  - Compare the on‑screen animation with the real Robot Arm to ensure the movement can be safely performed without colliding or moving unexpectedly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]
- Reduce joint accelerations/speeds if needed: normal operating loads can be reduced by lowering joint acceleration limits (this reduces dynamic loads that can contribute to abrupt behavior). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Secure and dimension the stand properly: ensure the mounting/stand is stiff and secure (insufficient stiffness or resonance can cause unexpected behavior or protective stops). Aim for minimum resonance frequency 45 Hz and follow the recommended mounting torque and methods. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

If more detail is needed (e.g., logs, program steps, whether a safety stop occurred), please provide that information so I can point to specific troubleshooting steps in the manuals.

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: This is likely a "singularity." A singularity is a pose that restricts the motion and ability to position the robot. If the arm is approaching a singularity it can stop moving or have very sudden and fast movements. This is likely an artifact of the program that is running. To prevent a singularity from occurring, avoid programming motions that result in any poses that could cause a singularity.
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the sources)
- Approaching a singularity: as the robot approaches a singularity pose it can stop moving or have very sudden and fast movements (singularity resistance increases and motion can become abrupt). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Stopping and restarting behavior / joint torques during stops: during stopping motion joints may exceed maximum nominal operating torque and generate high loads; improper handling of stops could lead to sudden motion when power/brakes change state. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Incorrect Move into Position or program start pose: Move Robot into Position can move the arm to an incorrect pose if TCP/feature/waypoint pose of the first movement was altered during execution or the first waypoint is inside an If/Switch node — unexpected repositioning could produce abrupt motion. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

How to prevent it (actions from the sources)
- Avoid singularities in programming and motion planning: do not program motions that result in poses that can cause a singularity. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Verify program start positions and use Move Robot into Position safely:
  - Ensure the robot is in the program’s first start position before playing programs.
  - Compare the on‑screen animation with the real Robot Arm to ensure the movement can be safely performed without colliding or moving unexpectedly. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]
- Reduce joint accelerations/speeds if needed: normal operating loads can be reduced by lowering joint acceleration limits (this reduces dynamic loads that can contribute to abrupt behavior). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Secure and dimension the stand properly: ensure the mounting/stand is stiff and secure (insufficient stiffness or resonance can cause unexpected behavior or protective stops). Aim for minimum resonance frequency 45 Hz and follow the recommended mounting torque and methods. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

If more detail is needed (e.g., logs, program steps, whether a safety stop occurred), please provide that information so I can point to specific troubleshooting steps in the manuals.

STUDENT ANSWER: Yes.

- Stop Category 0: Stop the robot by immediate removal of power. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]
- Stop Category 1: Stop the robot in an orderly, controlled manner; power is removed once the robot is stopped. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

QUESTION: I plugged in an active adapter, but nothing is showing up. What should I do?
STUDENT ANSWER: If you connected a Tool Cable Adapter while the robot was powered on, that can cause problems—always connect the adapter to the tool/end effector first, then to the robot, and do not power on the robot if the adapter is not connected to the tool/end effector [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

Steps to take now:
- Power down the robot before changing the adapter connections: use the Teach Pendant power button, unplug the mains cable, and wait ~30 seconds for stored energy to discharge [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].
- Connect the Tool Cable Adapter to the tool/end effector first, then to the robot tool connector, ensuring the connector is tightened (max 0.4 Nm) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].
- Verify tool power mode and I/O configuration in the Installation > Tool I/O settings in PolyScope (set internal power to 0V/12V/24V as appropriate) and check the Tool I/O electrical/spec limits before powering up [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

If problems persist, do not speculate—consult the end effector/tool documentation and ensure wiring and supply voltages match the robot Tool I/O specifications [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE (Three-Position Enabling) buttons are an enabling device used in Manual Mode: the button must be pressed and held in the center-on position to allow robot movement; releasing it causes a safeguard stop. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf] 

Supporting points:
- When a Three-Position Enabling Device is configured, movement in Manual Mode requires the 3PE to be pressed to the center-on position (and the robot will operate at Manual Reduced Speed unless High Speed Manual Mode is activated). [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]  
- The 3PE is used also to enable Backdrive (combined sequences require light-press and hold actions with the 3PE Teach Pendant or an external 3PE device). [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must conduct commissioning tests listed in the manual after making any modifications, including:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended.  
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended.  
- Observe the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the PolyScope screen.  
- Test the 3-position enabling device to verify pressing to the center enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops.  
- Test outputs tied to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode or Not Reduced Mode to verify the output changes are detected.  
- Determine and fulfill any additional commissioning requirements for your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Additionally, after maintenance/repair you must:
- Unplug main power and power off other energy sources; prevent others from powering the system during repair.  
- Check earth connection before re-powering; observe ESD precautions and prevent ingress of water/dust.  
- After maintenance/repair, perform checks to ensure the required safety level and correct functioning of all safety functions in accordance with national/regional work safety regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety parameter set that applies a distinct, more restrictive set of safety limits (e.g., joint position, joint speed, TCP pose/speed/force, momentum, power, stopping time/distance). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

When it is used:
- It is activated when the tool/end effector is positioned on the reduced side of a Trigger Reduced safety plane, or when an external safety input triggers Reduced Mode. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Triggered by a plane: there is a 20 mm transition band around the trigger plane where both normal and reduced limits are allowed to avoid nuisance stops. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- Triggered by an input: the robot adapts to the new limits within up to 500 ms after the input changes state. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

Additional note: Reduced Mode itself is a state change affecting safety function settings; it is not a standalone safety function. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

- Do not expose the robot to very high signal levels (e.g., welding environments can cause EMC problems).  
- Keep I/O cable lengths from the Control Box to other equipment ≤ 30 m unless additional tests are performed.  
- Use only the original cables supplied with the robot and avoid applications where those cables are subject to flexing.  
(See 008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__01__8.1._Electrical_Warnings_and_Cautions__pp59-60.pdf)

- Observe safety warnings: keep head and torso outside the robot workspace and do not place fingers where they can be caught; do not drive the robot into itself or anything else; stand clear and hold the emergency stop when playing movements for testing. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

QUESTION: What happens if my robot stopped in 1000ms when my stopping time safety limit is set to 200ms?
STUDENT ANSWER: The safety system enforces the configured Stopping Time Limit; if the robot takes 1000 ms to stop but the configured Stopping Time Limit is 200 ms, this constitutes a safety limit violation and the safety system will issue a Stop Category 0. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  

Supporting points:
- Stop Category 0 is initiated for a limit violation or safety system fault. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]  
- Recovery mode activates when a safety limit from the active set is violated; after a Stop Category 0 the safety system must be restarted and Recovery limits apply to allow moving the arm back within limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: How can I set up my active program so that I only need to modify 1 or 2 variables each run?
STUDENT ANSWER: You can use program and installation variables so the active program reads only a few values that you change each run.

- Create variables for the values you want to change (program variables belong to a program; installation variables belong to an installation and can be shared among programs). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

- Add variable descriptions (up to 120 characters) to clarify their purpose for operators in the Run tab. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

- Mark frequently changed variables as favorites (set Favorite variable in Program → Variable Setup for program variables, or Installation → General → Variables for installation variables). Then in Run, use "Show only favorite variables" to display just those few variables to edit before running. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

- When running, load the program (Run tab → Load Program), then edit the favorite variables in the Variables pane and press Play. The program will use the updated values at runtime. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

If you need the same values across multiple programs, use installation variables so you only change the shared installation variable once. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use Safety Planes and Tool Position (tool spheres) and enable elbow and/or tool flange restrictions in the safety configuration.

- Define a Plane feature in Installation > Features, then open Installation > Safety > Planes and Add plane. Configure the plane to restrict the area and enable "Restrict Elbow" and/or "Tool Flange" as required (you can configure up to eight planes) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

- Define the tool(s) under Installation > Safety > Tool Position: set the TCP position and radius (the robot treats the tool as a sphere when applying safety planes). The safety plane prevents any point on that tool sphere from crossing the plane; a reduced-mode trigger occurs if the sphere approaches a trigger plane [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

- Note: elbow restriction uses a defined elbow-sphere radius (0.13 m for UR5e) and only prevents the elbow sphere from passing through configured planes; safety planes limit the defined tool spheres and elbow, not other robot parts, so other parts may not be restricted by the plane [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf].

- Verify the application risk assessment and configure Normal/Reduced modes, since planes can be set to act in Normal, Reduced, Trigger Reduced, or both modes; also set Tool Position (otherwise plane triggers may not behave correctly) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

QUESTION: What are the limitations of using safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: The limitations of safety planes are:

- Safety planes limit robot position in space but only for the robot system (robot with its attached tool/end effector); they do not protect the end effector itself or monitor its functioning or connection cable [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  
- Safety planes take the expected stopping distance into account (the robot will slow down before the limit is reached), so stopping performance and stopping distance must be considered in the risk assessment (Stopping Time/Distance settings affect behavior) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Safety planes (and other configurable limits) are part of the robot’s safety system; if a safety-system fault or a limit violation is detected, the robot initiates a Stop Category 0 and all safety outputs reset to low—i.e., safety planes cannot compensate for faults in the safety system itself [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].  

If more detail is needed on configuring safety planes or how they interact with stopping distance/time, see the Safety Functions and Safety Parameter Set sections above [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: If the robot starts slowly or stops even when not near anything, the safety system is likely limiting motion or has entered Recovery mode due to a safety limit/violation or a configured Reduced mode trigger:

- The safety system will reduce speed or stop when configured safety limits (e.g., Speed Limit, Stopping Time/Distance, Safety Planes, Joint Position/Speed limits, Tool Orientation, Force, Momentum, Power) constrain motion; restricting stopping time/distance or other limits will reduce overall robot speed so it can stop within those limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

- The robot can be in Reduced mode (triggered by a Trigger Reduced Plane or a safety input) which uses more restrictive limits and will decelerate to satisfy them; transition can take up to 500 ms when triggered by an input [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

- If a safety limit has been violated or the robot was powered on while already outside a safety limit, Recovery mode is active: movement in Recovery is restricted by fixed limits (e.g., joint speed 30°/s, tool speed 250 mm/s, force 100 N, momentum 10 kg·m/s, power 80 W) and programs cannot run until recovery is cleared; joint/tool position and orientation limits are disabled in Recovery, so freedrive must be used cautiously to move back within limits [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf; 010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

Troubleshooting steps (based on the manual):
- Check whether the robot is in Reduced or Recovery mode on the Safety Configuration screens and verify which limit set is active [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- Inspect safety limits (speed, stopping time/distance, safety planes, joint limits) and the Safety Checksum to see if configuration changes were applied [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].
- If in Recovery, move the arm back within limits using Freedrive or Move tab (with caution) and then clear recovery so programs can run; note Recovery enforces fixed limits listed above [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

Sources: [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf], [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: Why does my robot arm look to be vibrating when running?
STUDENT ANSWER: Your robot arm may appear to be vibrating because the installation stand lacks sufficient dynamic stiffness or because the stand's eigenfrequency matches the robot motion frequency, causing resonance. (See "Dynamic stiffness" and resonance guidance.) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Supporting points:
- A stand that is not sufficiently stiff will deflect during robot motion, which can make the robot arm seem to vibrate and can also cause protective stops. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- The stand should have a minimum resonance frequency of 45 Hz to avoid resonant vibration with robot movements. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

STUDENT ANSWER: Use the built‑in safety functions that limit the robot’s energy transfer: set Force and Power limiting, Momentum limiting, and Speed limitation in the Safety Configuration so collisions produce lower forces and pressures.
