Supporting points:
- Force and power limiting reduce clamping forces and pressures from the tool/end effector during collisions [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Momentum limiting reduces transient energy/impact by lowering robot speed and momentum [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Speed limitation (tool/elbow speed limits) reduces impact energy and is configured under Robot Limits (Tool Speed, Elbow Speed) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf].

QUESTION: Are there risks associated with using 12V vs 24V?
STUDENT ANSWER: Yes — there are risks. The manual warns that programmer and/or wiring errors can cause the voltage to change from 12V to 24V, which can lead to fire damage to equipment, and it instructs to verify the use of 12V and proceed with caution [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

Also note tool power supply specifics and cautions:
- The Tool I/O internal power supply can be set to 0V, 12V or 24V; electrical specs (supply voltage, currents, soft-start behavior) must be followed to avoid damage (see Tool Power Supply and Tool I/O Installation Specifications) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].  
- A warning: connecting the Tool Cable Adapter to a powered robot can lead to injury; connect the adapter to the tool first and do not power on the robot if the adapter is not connected to the tool/end effector [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__07__8.7._End_Effector_Integration__pp84-96.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: The sudden strong movement after a stop is consistent with the robot approaching or exiting a singularity or with loads/torques during stops exceeding normal values — both can cause heavy, sudden motion. Relevant causes and prevention from the sources:

Possible causes
- Singularity: Approaching a singularity can make the robot resist motion and then move very fast or stop unexpectedly when the singularity is reached (6.3.1 Singularity Prevention) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Stopping loads / joint torque during stops: During stopping motion the joints may exceed maximum nominal operating torque; these higher loads can cause abrupt motion if not accounted for (6.2 Dimensioning the Stand — “During stopping motion, the joints are allowed to exceed the maximum nominal operating torque.”) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Inadequate mounting / unstable stand or insufficient stiffness: A stand that deflects or resonates can lead to unexpected robot behavior or protective stops that feel sudden (6.2 Dimensioning the Stand) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Collision or drive into restricted workspace (cylindrical volume): Moving the tool close to the cylindrical volume can cause joints to move too fast or lose functionality (6.1 Workspace and Operating Space) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

How to prevent recurrence
- Avoid programming motions that approach singularities; redesign paths to steer clear of singular poses (6.3.1 Singularity Prevention) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Ensure the mounting/stand is sturdy, vibration-free and dimensioned to withstand the robot’s torques and forces (verify capacities and use safety factors as described), and provide adequate static and dynamic stiffness (6.2 Dimensioning the Stand) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Securely mount the robot with the specified fasteners and torques, and verify stand can handle maximum loads during normal operation and stops (6.4 Securing the Robot Arm; 6.2 Dimensioning the Stand) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- Keep the robot tool away from the cylindrical volume above/below the base to prevent excessive joint speeds or loss of functionality (6.1 Workspace and Operating Space) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].  
- If high accelerations cause large loads, reduce joint acceleration limits in the program to lower operating loads (6.2 Dimensioning the Stand) [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf].

If these documents do not cover specific diagnostics for your incident, perform a risk assessment and review the program path, joint/acceleration settings, mounting integrity, and any protective stop or fault logs on the robot. The cited sections: 6.1, 6.2, 6.3.1 and 6.4 in 006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf.

STUDENT ANSWER: Yes.

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE (Three-Position Enabling) buttons are an enabling device that must be pressed and held in the center‑on position to allow robot motion in Manual Mode; releasing or fully compressing them causes a Safeguard Stop. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Supporting points:
- When a 3PE is used and the robot is in Manual Mode, movement requires the 3PE to be pressed and held in the center position to move the robot. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- If a 3PE is configured, the robot operates at Manual Reduced Speed unless High Speed Manual Mode is activated. Switching between Automatic and Manual requires the 3PE to be fully released and pressed again. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- The 3PE input is a dedicated safety input (paired for redundancy) and is intended for frequent use; it contributes to PLd performance and Stop Category 2 behavior. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__02__8.2._Safety_IO__pp61-70.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After modifying the robot arm you must perform the commissioning tests listed and maintenance/repair safety checks:

- Conduct the commissioning tests before using the robot application after any modifications:  
  - Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.  
  - Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots).  
  - Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.  
  - Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops (and if safeguard reset is configured, check it works).  
  - Verify initialization screen changes when activating reduced input.  
  - Change operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in PolyScope.  
  - Test the 3-position enabling device to verify center enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.  
  - If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify whole-system stop.  
  - Test outputs (Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, Not Reduced Mode) to verify detected changes.  
  - Determine any additional commissioning requirements for your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

- For maintenance/repair after modifying the robot arm, follow safety procedures and checks:  
  - Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources; prevent others from powering the system during repair.  
  - Check the earth (ground) connection before re-powering.  
  - Observe ESD regulations when parts are disassembled.  
  - Prevent water and dust ingress into the robot arm or Control Box.  
  - Do not disassemble the Control Box power supply too soon after switching off (high voltages up to 600 V may be present for hours).  
  - After maintenance/repair, perform checks to ensure the required safety level and correct functioning of all safety functions in accordance with national/regional work safety regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

- Perform post‑maintenance inspections per the Robot Arm Inspection Plan:  
  - Monthly/biannual/annual checks as recommended (e.g., flat rings, robot cable and connections, mounting bolts, tool mounting bolts, round sling).  
  - Move robot to ZERO, turn off and disconnect power, inspect cable between Control Box and Robot Arm, check base and tool flange mounting bolts, inspect flat rings and replace if worn/damaged.  
  - Never use compressed air to clean the robot arm.  
  - Verify Freedrive operation and that the arm can hold a manually moved position without activating Freedrive. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

If you need the exact step‑by‑step checklists or the Service Manual inspection plan for trained individuals, consult the Service Manual on Universal Robots’ documentation site as referenced in the maintenance document. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot; prevent others from restoring power during repair. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Check the earth/ground connection before re-powering the system. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Observe ESD (electrostatic discharge) regulations when parts are disassembled. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box; do not operate the Control Box in environments exceeding its IP rating. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf][006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Do not disassemble the Control Box power supply immediately after power‑off — high voltages (up to 600 V) can be present for several hours. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Use appropriate PPE and precautions when handling grease or cleaning agents (ventilation, gloves, eye protection); do not use bleach. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

Lock out and tag out main power (use a lockable OFF switch and residual current device as part of the electrical installation) and ensure no other equipment can supply power to robot I/O while serviced. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

After maintenance, verify correct functioning of all safety functions and adhere to national/regional work safety regulations; test safety functions before returning the system to operation. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

   - You can also hold the Freedrive button on the Teach Pendant and physically guide the arm to the desired positions.

QUESTION: My robot is close to a collision and if I restart it, it may cause another collision from the vibrations. What can I do?

- Ensure you operate only within Safety configuration and risk assessment; verify safety settings, and if needed, use Safe Home/Recovery guidance as context. QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?

- For each plane, you can restrict the Elbow and/or Tool Flange to prevent crossing the plane, ensuring the dangerous portions stay inside the allowed region. - If the tool or elbow approaches a safety plane, the safety system can switch to Reduced or Normal modes according to the plane configuration to enforce the boundary. - Ensure tool position is configured under Safety -> Tool Position and that a Tool Position is set so the safety planes can trigger correctly when the tool TCP approaches a plane. QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Answer: Check the safety configuration in PolyScope because the robot may be operating in Normal vs Reduced mode, or be in Recovery due to a prior safety limit violation. The safety system can slow or stop motion to stay within configured limits.

Key points from sources:
- Software Safety Modes define Normal, Reduced, and Recovery modes, with Reduced mode used when the TCP is in a reduced plane or triggered by safety inputs; Recovery mode restricts movement and disables certain limits until restored. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- Safety parameters (Normal vs Reduced) are configurable in Safety Configuration; ensure the current mode matches your risk assessment and that changes are applied. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]
- If a safety limit is violated, the system issues a Stop Category 0 or slows to meet stopping constraints; Recovery mode stops you from continuing until recovered. Verify Safety Checksum after changes to confirm settings. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

If you have confirmed risk assessment, also:
- Ensure you are not in Reduced mode due to a Trigger Plane or safety input. The Reduced configuration activates within 500 ms of a trigger; verify any safety inputs or planes configured to trigger reduced mode. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible cause: The robot arm may have reached a singularity or been commanded to move in a way that causes a sudden, large motion (singularity and stop conditions are discussed in Assembly safety sections). See 6.3.1 Singularity Prevention and general mounting/operation guidance. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

What to check and do:
- Check for singularity-prone poses in your program and avoid movements that approach singular configurations. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Ensure the installation and mounting are secure and that the stand is properly dimensioned and rigid to prevent unintended motions or vibrations. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Verify safe operating conditions and that you are not exceeding safety limits; review ISO 10218-1/ISO/TS 15066 guidance and ensure proper use of safety functions if in collaborative mode (e.g., SSM/PFL) as applicable. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

Prevention tips:
- Maintain secure mounting and proper stand stiffness to minimize dynamic resonances and unexpected stops. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Use appropriate programming practices: avoid moves that cause rapid or abrupt joint acceleration, and verify moves with a simulation or PolyScope Move Robot into Position guidance before running live. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]
- If operating in automatic mode with collaborative features, ensure safety functions like SSM and PFL are configured per the safety guidelines. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__02__19.2._Table_2__pp219-222.pdf]

Note: If the issue occurred during a move that could approach a singularity or during an unsafe configuration, power down and inspect mounting, configuration, and program flow before restoring operation. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Before performing maintenance on a UR robot arm, follow these main safety precautions:
- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box; ensure they cannot be powered on during maintenance. Check the earth connection before re-powering. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Observe ESD regulations and prevent water and dust ingress into the robot arm or Control Box. Use appropriate PPE (gloves, eye protection) when handling grease or contaminated areas. Do not use bleach in cleaning solutions. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Do not disassemble the power supply inside the Control Box; high voltages can remain after shutdown. Only repair work by Universal Robots or trained personnel following the Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Verify the earth connection and ensure all power sources are isolated before any inspection or repair. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- After maintenance, perform checks to confirm the required safety level and test the correct functioning of all safety functions per applicable regulations. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the risk of EMC interference, and how can it be avoided?
STUDENT ANSWER: EMC interference can cause unexpected robot behavior and log messages; very high signal levels or excessive exposure may permanently damage the robot. To avoid this:

- Use I/O cables within recommended lengths (not longer than 30 m) and ensure proper grounding and separation of safety signals from normal I/O signals. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-60.pdf]

STUDENT ANSWER: Use safety planes to define a boundary that restricts the elbow and, if needed, the tool flange. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Enable Elbow Restriction to prevent the elbow from crossing defined planes; enable Tool Flange Restriction to prevent the tool flange from crossing them.
- Plane features must be created in the Features screen and then copied into the safety Planes screen before activation. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: From the Safety Configuration and I/O sections:

- The robot may be limited by Safety Functions and Safety Modes (Normal vs Reduced vs Recovery). If Reduced mode is active, or a safety limit is violated, movement is slowed or stopped. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__03__10.3._Software_Safety_Configuration__pp107-120.pdf]

- If a safety limit is exceeded or a fault/violation is detected, the safety system triggers a Stop (Category 0 or 2). Recovery mode can disable some limits temporarily; movement is restricted there. - Ensure you have not triggered a Safety Input (e.g., Safety Planes, Reduced Mode plane, or external safety I/O) that forces reduced limits. Also confirm you’re operating with Normal Mode limits and that the safety configuration matches the risk assessment. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__01__10.2. Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- If you started from a Safe/Recovery state, the Move may be restricted until recovery or safety checks are cleared; use Freedrive or restore within safety limits as appropriate. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__01__10.2. Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- The 3PE device is also used to trigger Backdrive operations when combined with other backdrive methods (TP button or Freedrive), enabling manual joint movement during backdrive sequences. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Main safety precautions before maintenance:
- Unplug the main power cable from the bottom of the Control Box to ensure the system is completely unpowered, and power off any other energy sources connected to the robot arm or Control Box. Check the earth connection before re-powering. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Observe ESD regulations when disassembling any robot arm or Control Box parts. Prevent water and dust from entering the robot arm or Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Do not disassemble the power supply inside the Control Box quickly after switching off; high voltages can remain (up to 600 V). Avoid disassembling the power supply inside the Control Box. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Ensure the area is safe and that people are prevented from powering on the system during the repair period. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- Follow the latest Service Manual for inspection, calibration, and repair procedures; repairs should only be performed by Universal Robots or by client-designated, trained individuals under the Service Manual. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]
- After maintenance, perform checks to ensure the required safety level and test the correct functioning of all safety functions. [015__L1__15._Maintenance_and_Repair__pp192-204.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a safety state where all reduced mode safety limits are active. It can be entered by a safety plane trigger or by a safety input, and remains active until switched back.

- It affects safety function limits such as joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
- It is part of the Normal/Reduced safety parameter set and can be triggered by a safety plane (Trigger Reduced mode) or an external input, with a transition delay up to 500 ms if triggered by an input. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]
- It is not itself a safety function but a configuration state used to parametrize safety limits; the system transitions back to Normal when appropriate. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I lock the X axis from rotating on the arm when in freedrive mode?
STUDENT ANSWER: The Freedrive panel lets you lock axes to constrain movement. To prevent rotation about the X axis, lock axes so motion is limited to translation or a plane that excludes that rotation:

- In the Freedrive panel, choose "Plane" (movement only through X and Y) or "Translation" (movement allowed through all axes without rotation). Either option prevents rotation about the TCP (including rotation about X). [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

If needed, you can also lock individual axes using the axis list in the Freedrive panel to customize which axes are free. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

- Force/power limiting, momentum limiting and speed limitation can also reduce clamping forces, transient energy, or ensure speed stays below configured limits, which can make the arm move slowly or stop if limits are reached [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].
- Verify your safety configuration parameters and password protection (to ensure no unauthorized changes), since incorrect settings can cause reduced motion or unexpected stops [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes from the application risk assessment document:
- An item falling out of, or flying from, the tool/end effector (e.g., due to a poor grip or power interruption) which can create unexpected forces on the arm. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Incorrect setting of the safety configuration parameters or unauthorized changes to safety configuration (leading to unexpected behavior when limits or stopping settings are reached or changed). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Hazards related to stopping performance (if stopping limits or distance/time settings interact with motion limits, the robot can change speed or resume unexpectedly when limits are adjusted). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

How to prevent recurrence (actions recommended by the source):
- Conduct and complete the application risk assessment before first power-on and iteratively after installation; include teaching, troubleshooting, maintenance and normal operation. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Verify and set correct safety configuration settings and enable password protection to prevent unauthorized changes; manage passwords so only qualified persons can change settings. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Use appropriate safety functions for your application (force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limitation, joint/elbow/tool position and orientation limits) to limit energy transfer and avoid hazardous orientations. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- If hazards cannot be eliminated or reduced sufficiently by built‑in safety functions (for example when using a hazardous tool or process), add external safeguarding per ISO 10218‑2. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If the cause is not clear from these checks, perform a full application risk assessment looking at severity, likelihood and possibility to avoid the hazardous situation and address identified gaps. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What is the function of the 3PE buttons?
STUDENT ANSWER: The 3PE buttons are only active in Manual mode and have three positions with these functions: [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

- Position 1 — Release (not pressed): Robot movement is stopped in Manual mode; power is not removed and brakes remain released.  
- Position 2 — Light-press (pressed to middle point): Allows your program to play when the robot is in Manual mode.  
- Position 3 — Tight-press (fully pressed): Robot movement is stopped in Manual mode; robot is in 3PE Stop.

Additional behaviors:
- The 3PE buttons permit Freedrive when you rapidly light-press, release, then light-press and hold, letting you manually pull the arm while holding the light-press.  
- To run a program in Manual mode you must maintain a light-press; releasing the button stops or pauses the program. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use the Power terminal block inside the Control Box. By default the internal 24V supply powers the I/O (connects PWR and GND). If more current is needed, connect an external 24V supply to the lower two terminals (24V and 0V).

Key specs from the Control Box:
- Default (internal) 24V supply: PWR–GND = 24 V (typ), current up to 2 A (3.5 A for 500 ms or 33% duty cycle). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]
- External 24V input: 24V–0V = 24 V (typ), allowed 20–29 V, current up to 6 A. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]

Observe the terminal labeling: top pair = PWR, GND (internal supply); bottom pair = 24V, 0V (external supply). [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__04__8.4._Controller_IO__pp73-74.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform the commissioning tests listed before using the robot after any modifications. Specifically:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- On the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the PolyScope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test the 3-position enabling device: pressing to the center (on) position must enable motion in manual mode at a reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test any systems connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify the output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Determine and document the specific commissioning requirements for your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: The manual emphasizes reading and following the User Manual and treating all deviation from intended use as hazardous. Before performing maintenance:

- Read and follow the recommendations for intended use and the specifications in the User Manual. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]
- Do not modify the robot or e-Series end caps; only authorized disassembly/reassembly by a UR service center or skilled persons using the latest service manuals is permitted. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]
- Include added risks from reach, payload, operating torques and speeds in the application risk assessment — your risk assessment must cover the robot, end effector and workpiece. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

If these precautions are not followed, the manual warns misuse or improper maintenance can result in death, personal injury, and/or property damage. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state change (not a safety function) that activates a set of reduced safety function limits: joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. It is a means of parametrization of safety functions in accordance with ISO 13849‑1 and all parameter values must be verified and validated for the robot application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

Reduced Mode can be initiated either by a safety plane/boundary (it starts at 2 cm before the plane and reduced settings are achieved within 2 cm of the plane) or by use of an input to initiate (reduced settings achieved within 500 ms). STUDENT ANSWER: A pinch hazard is a workspace area where parts of the robot can create pinching injuries due to relative motion between robot parts or between the robot and obstacles. Universal Robots notes pinch-hazard areas include:
- Radial motions when the wrist 1 joint is at least 750 mm from the robot base.
- Tangential motions within 200 mm of the robot base.

5. Under Confirm new password, repeat your new password.

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: If the robot’s safety configuration includes limits that affect stopping or speed, the robot will reduce speed or stop automatically to ensure those limits are not exceeded. The safety functions that can cause slow movement or stopping include:

- Force & power limiting, momentum limiting, and speed limitation: these can reduce clamping forces, transient impacts, or overall speed and may make the arm move slowly even if no obstacle is nearby [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

Also check that safety configuration parameters were set correctly and not changed unintentionally (unauthorized or incorrect settings can cause unexpected behavior) [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Cause:
A likely cause is an issue related to stopping performance or incorrect safety configuration settings — for example the robot reached a configured stopping time or distance limit (or those limits were not correctly set), or an unauthorized/incorrect change to safety parameters allowed the robot to move unexpectedly. The sudden movement could also follow from hazards listed such as items flying from the end effector, loose bolts, or incorrect understanding/operation of multiple emergency stops. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

How to prevent it:
- Conduct an application risk assessment before first power-up and iteratively after installation to identify causes and required protections (including during teaching, troubleshooting and maintenance). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Use and correctly configure the built-in safety functions (force and power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limitation, joint/elbow/tool position and orientation limits) so the robot’s energy, speed and motions are limited to safe levels. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Configure Stopping Time Limit and/or Stopping Distance Limit so stopping performance is appropriate; when used, the safety control continuously monitors stopping so manual periodic stopping tests are not required. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Prevent unauthorized changes by enabling and setting password protection for the safety configuration and maintain a password-management program so only qualified persons can change settings. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Address mechanical risks that could cause sudden motions or releases: check for loose bolts, secure the tool/end effector and workpiece, and prevent items from falling or flying from the end effector. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If hazards cannot be eliminated or sufficiently reduced by built‑in safety functions (for example a hazardous tool or process), add appropriate safeguarding per ISO 10218-2. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

STUDENT ANSWER: The 3-Position Enabling (3PE) buttons control manual operation and freedrive of the robot in Manual mode only. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__05__8.5._Teach_Pendant_with_3-Position_Enabling_Device__pp75-82.pdf]

Supporting details:
- Position 1 (Release): no pressure — robot movement is stopped in Manual mode; power remains and brakes stay released.
- Position 2 (Light-press): some pressure — allows a program to play in Manual mode and is used to enable freedrive and to run/continue programs (hold light-press and tap Play/Resume).
- Position 3 (Tight-press): full pressure — robot movement is stopped in Manual mode (3PE Stop).
- Additional functions: rapid double light-press then hold enables Freedrive (you can manually move the arm while holding the light-press); light-press is used with Move Robot into Position and Automove to move the arm to a program start position. QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform the commissioning tests listed before using the robot after any modification. Specifically:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Check the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the PolyScope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test the 3-position enabling device to verify pressing to the center-on position enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test any systems connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify those output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Determine and document the specific commissioning requirements of your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state change that alters safety function limits (it is not itself a safety function). When in Reduced Mode, ALL reduced mode limits become active, affecting joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

Reduced Mode can be initiated by:
- a safety plane/boundary (activation starts at 2 cm from the plane and reduced mode settings are achieved within 2 cm), or
- an input signal (reduced settings are achieved within 500 ms) — when the external connections are Low, Reduced Mode is initiated. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After modifying the robot arm, perform the commissioning tests to verify safety and operation.

Key checks include:
- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected, and test them functioning as intended.
- Test emergency stop buttons/inputs to ensure the robot stops and brakes engage.
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; verify safeguard reset if configured.
- Check initialization screen (activate reduced input) and verify screen changes.
- Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in the PolyScope top-right.
- Test the 3-position enabling device to ensure center position enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press E-Stop to verify a system-wide stop.
- Test outputs such as Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode to ensure changes are detected.
- Determine the commissioning requirements for your specific robot application.

Source: 009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Based on the risk assessment and safety configuration guidance, the robot may move slowly or stop due to safety configuration settings. Ensure you have correctly configured the following:

- Safety configuration settings (e.g., speed limitation, momentum limiting, force/power limiting) are set according to the risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- Stopping performance controls (Stopping Time Limit and Stopping Distance Limit) may automatically constrain motion; if enabled, they reduce speed to stay within limits and the safety control performs continuous monitoring. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- Unauthorized changes to safety configuration should be prevented with password protection; incorrect settings can lead to unintended motion behavior. Verify password protection is enabled and configured properly. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If the issue persists after confirming these settings, re-check the risk assessment implementation and the applicability of any collaborative-mode controls. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: Power the control box from its internal 24V supply by default, or use an external 24V supply if more current is needed.

- The internal power supply provides 24V between PWR and GND; use this unless you require higher current.
- If using an external supply, connect 24V to the 24V and 0V of the external input terminals, with PWR/GND still tied as the internal reference.
- The external input can supply 20–29 V and 0 A up to 6 A (typical 24V). It supports up to 3.5A for 500 ms or 33% duty cycle.

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: After modifying the robot arm, perform the commissioning checks listed in the document:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected.
- Test all connected safety input and output (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) are functioning as intended.
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
- Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops; if safeguard reset is configured, check that it functions as intended.
- Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
- Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in the top right corner of the PolyScope screen.
- Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify a stop of the whole system.
- Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
- Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What safety modes does the robot arm have?
STUDENT ANSWER: The robot arm has the following safety-related operational modes: Automatic Mode, Manual Mode (including High Speed Manual Mode), Recovery Mode, Freedrive (a Manual Mode/Backdrive-related state), Backdrive, and Reduced mode (as part of Normal/Reduced safety parameter sets). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf] [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Automatic Mode: executes predefined programs; no program modification permitted. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Manual Mode: allows programming and saving; includes High Speed Manual Mode (temporary speed exceedance with hold-to-run) and may operate at Reduced Speed when a Three-Position Enabling Device is configured. [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Recovery Mode: a type of Manual Mode activated when a safety limit is exceeded; programs cannot run and limits are relaxed to allow moving the arm back within limits. - Freedrive and Backdrive: modes to manually move the arm (Freedrive enables manual movement; Backdrive releases specific joint brakes for heavy manual movement). [013__L1__13._Emergency_Events__pp181-189.pdf]
- Reduced mode: part of the Normal/Reduced safety parameter set that applies lower limits when triggered by plane or safety input. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

QUESTION: How can I set up my active program so that I only need to modify 1 or 2 variables each run?
STUDENT ANSWER: You can expose the few variables you need by using Installation variables (shared) or Program variables and marking them as favorites so they’re easy to change in Run.

Steps (from the source):
- Create the variables you need as Program variables (belong to the program) or Installation variables (shared among programs) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf].  
- Add descriptions to the variables to convey their purpose (up to 120 characters) so operators know what to modify [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf].  
- Designate the one or two variables you will change as Favorite variables:
  - For program variables: Header → Program → Variable Setup → select variable → check Favorite variable [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf].  
  - For installation variables: Header → Installation → General → Variables → select variable → check Favorite variable [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf].  
- In the Run tab, enable Show only favorite variables to display only those favorites for quick modification before running the program [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf].

This lets operators change only the 1–2 designated variables from the Run screen before Play, keeping the rest of the program unchanged. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__05__10.5._The_First_Program__pp133-162_part01.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot is close to a collision and if I restart it, it may cause another collision from the vibrations. What can I do?
STUDENT ANSWER: The manual advises performing a risk assessment and installing safeguarding or configuring safety settings to prevent collisions; specifically, use safety configuration settings (e.g., stopping time/distance limits, speed limitation, force/momentum limiting, and joint/tool position limits) and safeguarding if built‑in functions cannot sufficiently reduce the risk. Also ensure password protection to prevent unauthorized changes to safety settings. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf] [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Short actionable items based on the sources:
- Configure stopping performance limits (Stopping Time Limit or Stopping Distance Limit) so the robot safety control continuously monitors and limits motion to prevent further collisions. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Apply speed, force/power, and momentum limiting to reduce energy and impact if unintended motion occurs on restart. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Use joint, elbow and tool position/orientation limiting or additional safeguarding to prevent movement into the hazardous area where vibration could cause contact. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Perform a (re)risk assessment for the situation and, if required, install physical safeguarding or prevent restart until the hazard is removed. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: If the robot is moving slowly or stopping even when not near anything, it may be because one or more safety configuration limits are active (these automatically affect robot speed to ensure limits are not exceeded). Relevant possibilities include:

- Stopping Time Limit or Stopping Distance Limit in the safety configuration: when these limits are used the robot safety control continuously monitors and automatically reduces speed to ensure the configured stopping time/distance is not exceeded [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Force/power limiting, momentum limiting, or speed limitation settings: these functions reduce speed, force or momentum (and thus movement) to limit energy transfer in case of collisions and can make the arm move slower [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Joint, elbow or tool/end effector position or orientation limits: position/orientation limiting can prevent movements toward certain areas and thus restrict motion or stop it [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  

Also ensure safety configuration parameters have not been changed (unauthorized changes can produce incorrect settings) and that password protection is enabled to prevent inadvertent modifications [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]. If these settings are not the cause, the integrator/user must validate the application design and safety settings per the risk assessment and integration responsibilities listed in the safety manual [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf].

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the sources)
- The robot entered Freedrive (brakes released) while it was being moved or pushed, which can cause the robot to drift or behave unexpectedly and can lead to faults or sudden motion. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- The robot was moved near a predefined limit, plane, or singularity in Freedrive; resistance then increases and the arm can behave heavily or stop and resume abruptly. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- During initialization, brakes are released and minor vibrations or unwanted motion can occur; using Backdrive incorrectly or not using it when appropriate can produce unexpected movements. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

How to prevent it happening again
- Do not enable Freedrive while you are pushing or touching the robot; enable Freedrive only when you intend to move the arm manually. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Verify the configured payload matches the actual payload and that the payload is securely attached before enabling Freedrive or moving the robot. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- When in Freedrive, be aware of approach to joint limits, planes and singularities (resistance increases and motion can become heavy or stop); avoid pulling through singularities and use the "All axes are free" control in the Freedrive panel to resume movement safely. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- During initialization or when vibrations/undesired movements occur, use Backdrive to force specific joints to a desired position without releasing all brakes rather than releasing all brakes unintentionally. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

If these measures do not explain or prevent the event, conduct the application risk assessment and verify installation, payload and safety configuration as part of troubleshooting. The integrator/user is responsible for the application risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: 1. Connect the robot cable from the robot arm to the Control Box and lock the connector (twist twice) before powering on. Do not extend or modify the original Robot Cable. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

2. Plug the mains (power) cable into the IEC C14 inlet at the bottom of the Control Box using the supplied IEC power cord with a country‑specific wall plug (do not use an adapter). Ensure the Control Box is grounded. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

3. Provide the required electrical protections and switches as part of the installation: main fuse, Residual Current Device (RCD), and a lockable main switch (lockable in OFF position) to allow full lockout. Use appropriate fuse ratings per input voltage (see electrical specs). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

4. Powering sequence/precautions:
   - Turn on the robot using the Teach Pendant power button after the mains is connected.  
   - Do not disconnect the Robot Cable while the robot arm is turned on.  
   - If mounting or servicing, power down first: press the Teach Pendant power button to turn off, unplug the mains cable, and wait 30 seconds for stored energy to discharge. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must conduct the commissioning tests listed in the commissioning checklist before using the robot application after any modifications. Specifically:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test that all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices shared between machines/robots) function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- On the initialization screen, activate the reduced mode input and verify the screen changes. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the Polyscope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test the 3-position enabling device: pressing to the center position must enable motion in manual mode at reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Test any systems connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify the output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]
- Determine and document the specific commissioning requirements for your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Additionally, ensure you have performed an application risk assessment after physical installation and integration (required before first power-on or after modifications), including setting appropriate safety configuration settings and password protection. The integrator is responsible for the risk assessment per ISO 12100/ISO 10218-2; consider force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limits, joint/tool position/orientation limits, and stopping time/distance settings as part of that process. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Set and follow the intended-use instructions and read the manual; do not use the robot outside intended uses. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

Enable password protection on safety configuration to prevent unauthorized changes (manage passwords so only qualified persons can change settings). [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Identify and configure appropriate safety functions and limits (force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limits, stopping time/distance, joint/elbow/tool position and orientation limits) as determined by the risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Do not modify the robot or e‑series end caps; authorized disassembly/assembly must be done at a UR service center or per current service manuals by skilled persons. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

Address physical hazards before maintenance: remove obstacles that create pinch hazards or use safety planes/joint limits to prevent the robot moving into hazardous workspace areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Additional cautions from the manual:
- Consider risks from reach, payload, torque and speed in the risk assessment. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]
- If hazards from the tool/process cannot be sufficiently reduced by built‑in safety functions, provide external safeguarding per ISO 10218‑2. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state change that alters safety function limits (joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance); it is not itself a safety function but a parametrization of safety functions per ISO 13849-1. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

When used:
- It can be initiated by a safety plane/boundary (starts at 2 cm from the plane and reaches the reduced settings within 2 cm) or by an input (reaches reduced settings within 500 ms).  
- Reduced Mode is active when the configured external connections are Low.  
- All reduced mode limits become active when Reduced Mode is initiated; parameter values must be verified and validated for the robot application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

- If transporting or moving the robot without original packaging, fold the robot as much as possible (do not transport extended or in the singularity position), move the center of gravity as close to the base as possible, and secure each tube to a solid surface at two different points; secure any attached end effector rigidly in 3 axes. Follow these precautions when manually moving or checking the arm’s position stability: hold both tubes, avoid extended/singularity positions, ensure base mounting bolts are tight, and confirm correct mounting orientation in the Installation settings. QUESTION: What happens if my robot stopped in 1000ms when my stopping time safety limit is set to 200ms?
STUDENT ANSWER: The safety system enforces the configured Stopping Time Limit (200 ms) by dynamically reducing robot speed so it can always be stopped within that limit; if a safety limit is exceeded (including stopping time), the safety system reaction is a Stop Category 0 (immediate removal of power) or a Stop Category per trigger. The document states that a Limit Violation or Fault Detection causes a Stop Category 0 [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

- If a safety limit is violated (e.g., the robot actually required 1000 ms to stop when the limit is 200 ms), the safety system will detect the violation and initiate Stop Category 0 (immediate removal of power) [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf].

QUESTION: I used to use an old robot arm, which I had to constantly test the stopping performance for every use, do I have to do that with this arm?

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: Use safety planes, elbow restrictions, and tool flange/tool position limits in the Safety configuration.

Key steps:

Copy the plane feature into a safety plane and set its Restrictions and Mode (Normal, Reduced, Trigger Reduced, etc.). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

- Enable "Restrict Elbow" on the safety plane to prevent the robot elbow joint from passing through the plane (elbow sphere radii listed for UR5e = 0.13 m). - Restrict the tool flange (or leave it unrestricted) and define Tool Position(s) (Installation > Safety > Tool Position). Set the tool TCP position and a tool sphere radius so safety planes and triggers correctly consider the tool geometry; the safety system prevents any point on the defined tool sphere from crossing a safety plane. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__04__10.4._Software_Safety_Restrictions__pp121-132.pdf]

Notes:
- Safety planes only limit the defined Tool sphere and elbow, not other parts of the arm; verify other arm parts cannot enter hazardous areas by risk assessment. QUESTION: What risks do I need to be aware of for the safety planes?
STUDENT ANSWER: Safety planes limit robot position and can affect stopping behavior; risks to be aware of include:

- Limit violation causes an immediate Stop Category 0 (robot stops without monitored deceleration) if a safety plane is exceeded. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- Safety planes take expected stopping distance into account: the robot motion will slow down before the plane is reached, and Stopping Time/Stopping Distance limits dynamically reduce speed so the robot can be stopped within configured limits. Include stopping time/distance in your risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- Incorrect configuration or unauthorized changes to safety planes (or other safety parameters) can leave hazards uneliminated or insufficiently reduced—always set password protection and perform an application risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- In Recovery mode safety planes and other limits are disabled; manually moving the arm back within limits can be hazardous—use caution. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-164__L2__02__10.2._Safety-related_Functions_and_Interfaces__pp99-106.pdf]

- Pinch hazards: certain workspace areas (near the base or radial motions with wrist extended) require attention—use safety planes and joint limits to prevent the robot from moving into pinch-hazard areas. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: My robot arm stopped moving and then had a strong, sudden movement. What could have caused this? How can I prevent this from happening again?
STUDENT ANSWER: Possible causes (from the sources)
- The robot entered Freedrive while you were moving or pushing the arm, which can cause the arm to drift and lead to faults; this can result in unexpected or sudden movement when brakes are released or re-engaged. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- The robot approached a predefined limit, plane, joint limit or singularity while in Freedrive; resistance increases and the robot can stop moving or behave abruptly as it transitions near those limits. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- A mismatch in mounting or payload verification at start-up can disable Start or produce errors; incorrect payload/installation can cause unexpected behaviour when brakes are released. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- If safety configuration or limits (stopping time/distance, speed, force/momentum limits, joint/elbow/tool limits) are incorrectly set or changed (especially by unauthorized access), stopping or limiting behaviour can change unexpectedly. The risk assessment warns that incorrect or unauthorized safety configuration can increase risks. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

How to prevent it (recommended actions from the sources)
- Do not enable Freedrive while you are pushing or touching the robot; enable Freedrive only when intended (use 3PE Teach Pendant sequence, Freedrive on robot button or I/O Actions). [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Verify the configured payload and that the correct payload is securely attached before freeing or starting the robot; ensure installation and payload settings are correct. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Avoid enabling Freedrive during movement; enabling while moving can cause drift leading to faults. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Be aware of and monitor joint limits, singularity and software safety restrictions when using Freedrive; use the Freedrive panel indicators and lock axes appropriately to limit motion. [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]
- Conduct an application risk assessment and set appropriate safety configuration settings (force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limits, joint/elbow/tool limits, stopping time/distance) and protect those settings with password protection to prevent unauthorized changes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If these sources do not fully explain your specific event, perform a risk assessment and review Freedrive, payload/installation settings, safety configuration and system logs for the incident. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf] [007__L1__7._First_Boot__pp52-58.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I power up the control box?
STUDENT ANSWER: Power up the Control Box by connecting the mains cable and supplying mains power, then turning on the robot from the Teach Pendant. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Steps / key requirements:
- Connect the IEC C13 on the supplied power cord to the IEC C14 inlet at the bottom of the Control Box and plug the country‑specific mains plug into the wall (do not use an adapter). [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Ensure the robot is grounded, protected by a residual current device (RCD) and correct main fuse, and that a lockable switch is installed for lockout. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- After connecting the Robot Cable to the arm and Control Box and verifying cables are correct and locked, press the power button on the Teach Pendant to turn the robot on. Allow 30 seconds after unplugging before servicing to discharge stored energy. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

Warnings:
- Always use the supplied/original power cord with a country‑specific plug; do not use adapters. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]
- Do not power the Control Box without proper grounding, RCD/fuse protection, and ensuring no other equipment supplies power to the robot I/O when locked out. [006__L1__6._Assembly__pp38-51.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: You must perform the commissioning tests listed for use after making any modifications. In particular:

- Verify all safety inputs and outputs are correctly connected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test all connected safety inputs and outputs (including devices common to multiple machines/robots) to confirm they function as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test all emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; if a safeguard reset is configured, check it functions as intended. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Check the initialization screen, activate the reduced mode input and verify the screen changes. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the top-right corner of the PolyScope screen. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test the 3-position enabling device: pressing to the center position must enable motion in manual mode at reduced speed. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and verify the whole system stops. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Test any system connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode outputs to verify those output changes are detected. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]  
- Determine and document the commissioning requirements specific to your robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

Additionally, before powering on after modification you must have performed an application risk assessment (integrator responsibility) addressing safety configuration, hazards introduced by the tool/end effector or environment, and required safeguarding per ISO 12100/ISO 10218-2 (and ISO/TS 15066 guidance for collaborative applications). Set and protect safety configuration passwords to prevent unauthorized changes. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Do an application risk assessment, follow the User Manual, and not modify the robot; set password protection for safety settings. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

Supporting points:
- Conduct an application risk assessment before any work (including maintenance) that considers tasks such as troubleshooting and maintenance, severity, likelihood, and possibility to avoid the hazardous situation, using ISO 12100 and ISO 10218-2 as guidance [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Never modify the robot or e-Series end caps; authorized disassembly/reassembly must be done at a UR service center or per the latest service manuals by skilled persons [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf].  
- Use the risk assessment to determine required safety configuration settings (and enable password protection to prevent unauthorized changes) because incorrect or unauthorized changes to safety parameters can cause injury or death [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].  
- Verify that hazards associated with reach, payload, torques, speeds, tools/end effectors, obstacles and other machines are identified and mitigated (e.g., by using joint limits, safety planes, or other safeguarding) before maintenance [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf] [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf].

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state change that alters safety function parameter settings so that all reduced-mode limits are active (joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance). It is a means of parametrizing safety functions in accordance with ISO 13849-1 and is not itself a safety function. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

Reduced Mode is initiated either by:
- a safety plane/boundary (it starts at 2 cm from the plane and reduced settings are achieved within 2 cm), or
- an external input (reduced settings are achieved within 500 ms) — specifically when the configured external connections transition to Low. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

Supporting notes:
- All parameter values used in Reduced Mode must be verified and validated as appropriate for the robot application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the external connection ports on the robot?
GROUND TRUTH ANSWER: Teach Pendant Port, SD Card slot, Ethernet, USB 2.0 and USB 3.0, Mini Displayport, 10A Mini Blade Fuse
STUDENT ANSWER: The external connection ports are on the underside of the I/O interface groups, with capped openings at the base of the Control Box cabinet to run external cables to access the ports. The Ethernet interface is available for MODBUS, EtherNet/IP, and PROFINET, remote access/control, and is connected by passing the cable through the base and using a cable gland. Active adapters and proper grounding per instructions are required. Also, the system supports an external Three-Position Enabling device or a 3PE Teach Pendant (via configurable inputs), and there is an Operational Mode switch required when using enabling devices. [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]

QUESTION: How do I ensure the robot elbow and tool remain within a certain area/boundary?
STUDENT ANSWER: To keep the elbow and tool within a defined area, use safety planes and elbow/tool flange restrictions in the Safety configuration.

- Configure safety planes (up to eight) to limit the workspace for the Tool and Elbow and optionally restrict elbow movement and the tool flange. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-132.pdf]
- Enable Elbow Restriction and Tool Flange Restriction so the elbow and tool cannot cross defined safety planes. The elbow restriction radius depends on robot size (UR5e: 0.13 m). [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-132.pdf]
- Add and configure a plane feature with displacement offsets as needed, and use the Plane’s normal to position the boundary. Tool Direction and Tool Position restrictions further help keep the tool within safe limits. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-132.pdf]

If you need, I can guide you through adding a specific safety plane and enabling elbow/tool restrictions step by step. [010__L1__10._First_Time_Use__pp98-132.pdf]

QUESTION: Why is the robot arm moving slowly or stopping when I start it? It is not near anything and I have done a risk assessment.
STUDENT ANSWER: Based on the risk assessment and safety configuration information, if the robot arm moves slowly or stops when starting, check the safety configuration settings and stopping performance settings that may limit speed or stopping behavior.

Key points to review:
- Safety configuration settings include energy/force/power limiting, momentum limiting, speed limiting, and orientation/position limits. These can slow or restrict motion to reduce risk. Ensure they are set appropriately for the application. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Stopping performance: stopping time limit and stopping distance limit can affect motion if active, as the safety control continuously monitors and enforces configured limits. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- For collaborative or safeguarded setups, ensure that safeguarding and correct safety settings are in place as determined by the risk assessment; incorrect or unauthorized changes to safety configuration can cause reduced speed or stops. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

If the issue persists after confirming these settings, consult the integrator responsibilities to verify that the correct safety configuration parameters are set and not modified unintentionally. [003__L1__3._Safety__pp28-32.pdf]

- Conduct a proper risk assessment prior to powering on the robot for the first time and after changes, to configure stopping performance and other protective measures appropriate to the task. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

- If hazards cannot be eliminated by built-in safety functions, implement safeguarding per ISO 10218-2, and review the potential pinch/impact hazards identified in the risk assessment. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

QUESTION: What check procedures do I need to follow after modifying the robot arm?

- Test all connected safety I/O, including devices common to multiple machines/robots.
- Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and brakes engage.
- Test safeguard inputs to verify robot motion stops; check that safeguard reset functions if configured.
- Review the initialization screen, activate the reduced input, and verify the screen changes.
- Change the operational mode and verify the mode icon changes in the PolyScope top-right.
- Test the 3-position enabling device to ensure pressing center enables motion in manual mode at reduced speed.
- If Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the E-Stop and verify a system stop.
- Test outputs connected to Robot Moving, Robot Not Stopping, Reduced Mode, or Not Reduced Mode to verify output changes are detected.
- Determine commissioning requirements for your specific robot application. [009__L1__9._Commissioning__pp97-97.pdf]

QUESTION: What are the main safety precautions that should be taken before performing maintenance on a Universal Robot Arm?
STUDENT ANSWER: Key safety precautions from the retrieved sources:

- Perform an application risk assessment before powering the robot for the first time, and ensure safety configuration settings are determined accordingly. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Enable and use password protection to prevent unauthorized changes to safety configuration. Always set up a password management process so access is restricted to qualified personnel. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]
- Do not modify the robot or end caps; any disassembly/reassembly should be performed by a UR service center or per the latest service manuals by skilled persons. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]
- Consider risks related to reach, payload, operating torques and speeds; ensure the risk assessment accounts for these factors during maintenance planning. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]
- For collaborative-safe applications, ensure safety configurations (including limiting forces, momentum, speed, and orientation) are set according to the risk assessment; improper settings can cause injury. [004__L1__4._Risk_Assessment__pp33-36.pdf]

Notes:
- If the robot is used in a collaborative context, ensure protective measures and the safety configuration are properly configured before maintenance. [001__L1__1._Liability_and_Intended_Use__pp10-11.pdf]

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state where all reduced safety function limits are ACTIVE, affecting joint position, joint speed, TCP pose limit, TCP speed, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. QUESTION: What are the external connection ports on the robot?
STUDENT ANSWER: The external connection ports are on the underside of the I/O interface groups and include Ethernet and display/monitor connections via the Control Box. The Ethernet port supports MODBUS, EtherNet/IP, PROFINET, and remote access/control; use a cable through the base hole and replace the base cap with a cable gland [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]. There is also a Mini Displayport for monitors (requires an active Mini DisplayPort to DVI/HDMI converter; passive adapters do not work) [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]. Additionally, the Fuse must be UL marked Mini Blade type (10A max, 32V min) and the Teach Pendant should be powered off before connecting to the Control Box to avoid damage [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__03__8.3._Control_Box_Connection_Ports__pp71-72.pdf]. For three-position enabling, the system supports a 3PE Teach Pendant or external three-position enabling device connected to the corresponding CI inputs, with an Operational Mode switch required [008__L1__8._Installation__pp59-96__L2__06__8.6._Three_Position_Enabling_Device__pp83-83.pdf].

Test all connected safety input and output, including devices common to multiple

Test emergency stop buttons and inputs to verify the robot stops and the brakes engage.
Test safeguard inputs to verify the robot motion stops. If safeguard reset is configured,
check that it functions as intended.
Look at the initialization screen, activate the reduced input and verify the screen changes.
Change the operational mode to verify the mode icon changes in top right corner of
PolyScope screen.
Test the 3-position enabling device to verify that pressing to the center on position enables
motion in manual mode at a reduced speed.
If the Emergency Stop outputs are used, press the Emergency Stop push-button and
verify that there is a stop of the whole system.
Test the system connected to Robot Moving output, Robot Not Stopping output, Reduced
Mode output, or Not Reduced Mode output to verify the output changes are detected.
Determine the commissioning requirements of your robot application.

QUESTION: What is Reduced Mode? When is it used?
STUDENT ANSWER: Reduced Mode is a state where all reduced mode safety limits are ACTIVE, affecting joint position, joint speed, TCP pose/speed limits, TCP force, momentum, power, stopping time, and stopping distance. It can be initiated by a safety plane/boundary (starting within 2 cm) or by an input (reaching reduced settings within 500 ms) and is entered when external connections are Low. It is not a safety function itself, but a parametrization of safety function limits in accordance with ISO 13849-1; all parameter values must be verified for the specific application. [019__L1__19._Safety_Functions_Table__pp211-222__L2__01__19.1._Table_1a__pp218-218.pdf]
